bonuses.requirements: U.S. Personal Savings Rate Falls to 4.2% in September, Lowest Since October 2022HomeFeedNewsU.S. Personal Savings Rate Falls to 4.2% in September, Lowest Since October 2022U.S. Personal Savings Rate Falls to 4.2% in September, Lowest Since October 202210/31 20:45On November 1, The Kobeissi Letter reported that the U.S. personal savings rate declined by 0.2 percentage points to 4.2% in September, marking the lowest level since October 2022. Since January 2024, the personal savings rate has decreased by a total of 3.4 percentage points. Currently, the savings rate is significantly below the pre-pandemic average of 6.2% over the past five years. Meanwhile, personal income in the U.S. grew by 4.1% year-on-year in September, the second-lowest growth rate since April 2022. During the same period, personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased by 6.3% year-on-year, the second-highest year-on-year increase since December 2024. In other words, the growth rate of consumer spending continues to outpace income growth, further squeezing household savings and increasing reliance on borrowing. Real-time news, insights, prices, trending stories, and expert analysis - all in one place.Who Can Stop the Tech Stock Decline? Nomura: The Midterm Elections Won't Help, Only the Fed CanNomura strategist Naka Matsuzawa argues that the U.S. midterm elections will not be the catalyst that ends the global tech selloff, contrary to widespread market hopes. In his October 30 macro strategy note, he contends that election results matter far less to equities than expected, and that the only real catalyst capable of halting the tech decline is the Federal Reserve ending its rate-hiking cycle.

Matsuzawa attributes tech weakness not to election uncertainty but to two deeper drivers: mounting concerns over the sustainability of AI investment and persistent credit worries. He notes that event premiums around the midterms in futures markets have already fallen noticeably, and that companies expected to face tighter regulation have not visibly underperformed—evidence that the selloff is not directly tied to regulatory fears. Investors, he observes, are punishing earnings misses harshly while giving little credit to beats, and they favor restrained capex, improved cash flow and shareholder returns over aggressive spending, reflecting deep anxiety about an AI investment slowdown.

Recent sector moves—a rebound in semiconductors (SOX up 6.9% for the week) alongside weakness in hyperscalers and software—do not, in his view, constitute meaningful rotation, since capital goods and machinery stocks, typically leading indicators of AI investment recovery, remain subdued. In rates, he attributes divergent long-end moves to differing central bank tones: the Fed was more dovish than expected, the ECB signaled a December hike, and the BoJ raised inflation forecasts.
